visible_text: One GRPO step on one GPU

Six stages repeat every step on one DGX Spark GB10 with Qwen3-0.6B. Prompts go to the SGLang engine, which writes 256 answers in 47.5 s. A math reward scores each answer. The FSDP trainer computes log probabilities in 23.4 s, then takes the gradient step in 77.0 s. Together they are the training phase of 100.3 s. A weight update of 0.64 s gives the engine the new weights. Medians of 48 steps of a run made before we added the heat guard, so no pause could occur.
ONE STEP, MEDIAN OF 48 STEPS, RUN BEFORE THE HEAT GUARD
152.6 s in all. Training takes the most time, and the weight update the least.
Engine and trainer take turns on the same GPU memory.

visible_text: A dead engine does not stop the job

Two runs on one time axis. Without a watchdog, the engine stopped at start, and the rollout loop then logged 200,533 HTTP 503 errors over 63 minutes while the GPU did nothing, until we stopped the container. With watchdog.sh, a test container that logged the same error without a break stopped after 183 seconds, when six checks in a row found more than 100 errors. A healthy 16-answer run logged bursts of this error of up to 60 seconds, two of them 45 seconds apart. A replay of that run stopped it in more than half of the cases with six checks and in none with ten, so we run the watchdog with ten.
more than 100 errors in six checks
Start every unattended run with a watchdog. The job alone never fails.
Healthy bursts came 45 s apart, so six checks are too few. Run it with ten.

A FlashAttention 3 error means a GPU that is not Hopper, because the FA3 build in the image is for Hopper only. A Ray out-of-memory error means the node was full. Step times that differ mean heat pauses. A rejected trainer attention name means a name that the installed transformers library does not accept.
Section 7.1 has every symptom we hit, and six more from issue reports.

visible_text: Two fixes for two different halves

The trainer and the engine compute the same model with different kernels, so their log probabilities differ. Deterministic inference fixes only the engine half: the same input gives the same output for any batch. True on-policy mode fixes the gap itself by making both sides run the same kernels, which works only where its contract holds: FlashAttention 3 on Hopper GPUs, compute capability 9.0, and Qwen3 dense models.
its own matmul and sum order
gap stays about 0.015 in our runs
gap goes to zero, where the contract holds

FlashAttention 3 on both sides, Hopper GPUs only
A GB10 is compute capability 12.1, so the contract does not start there.

visible_text: One GRPO step on one GB10

One DGX Spark GB10 package drawn in iso: a Grace CPU die with 20 Arm cores and a Blackwell GPU die, both joined to one 128 GB slab of unified LPDDR5X memory at the center. An NVLink-C2C link joins the two dies. On the Grace die run the Ray head, the TrainerController and RolloutExecutor Ray actors, and the math reward. On the Blackwell die the FSDP trainer is active and the SGLang engine waits. Inside the shared slab the trainer state is the active footprint and the engine state is parked. The trainer onloads its state from the slab in 0.87 s, and the weight update from the trainer to the parked engine state takes 0.64 s. Below, one median step of 152.6 s to scale: rollout 47.5 s, log probabilities 23.4 s, GRPO update 77.0 s, weight update 0.64 s, and 4.2 s that the phase medians do not cover. Medians of 48 steps of a run made before we added the heat guard.

LPDDR5X · 128 GB unified, one pool for both dies
